Hi all,

I am trying to warp a skull using WarpRefMesh, but I have come across some issues regarding my landmark coordinates. I have exported coordinates from IDAVs Landmark Editor as .pts, which I don't think can be read by geomorph, so I have also tried exporting as .dta, and corrected the header manually as stated in the manual. I am using a single scanned specimen for this analysis (I will be warping it to the min and max along PC axes). I use read.ply to read in the mesh (of the same scanned specimen) and mshape without issue.  However, I'm running into problems after this:

- if I use the command readmulti.nts, I get the error message straight away:
"Error in scan(file = file, what = "char", quote = "", sep = "\n", strip.white = TRUE,  :
  'file' must be a character string or connection"

- if I use readland.nts, I can read the points file in, but I get an error message when I then run WarpRefMesh:
"Error in digitspec[1:fixed, ] : incorrect number of dimensions"

I've attached a screenshot of the .dta file I manually changed the header of. It is one specimen with 49 landmarks x 3 dimensions (=147). I can only assume it is a problem with the .dta file. It is also very strange readland.nts (for multiple specimens) reads in ok, but readmulti.nts (for a single specimen) doesn't work.

Has anyone got any advice on what the error messages mean or how to proceed?

Cheers!
Kirilee

messages.body_plain:
Dear Kirilee,

I have to preface this by saying that I have never used readmulti.nts. However, according to the help file, this function "reads multiple *.nts files, each containing landmark coordinates for a single specimen". So, I would guess you would need to only use this function if you have multiple files, for one specimen. readland.nts seems to be what you need to use (but someone should correct me if I am totally wrong on this)

Concerning your second problem with readland.nts, are you certain that objects you are entering for the the "mesh.coord" and "ref" are matrices? Readland.nts creates an array. Before you can use this data in warpRefMesh, you need to subset this array first.
If this is not done, I would dare to gues that this gives you the error that pertains to the number of dimensions.

Without a reproducible example, I tried to get your error with the scallop data from the geomorph package If I use code snippet A, I do get your error. However, when I use code snippet B, I do not get your error and the function works as intended. See how I specified a single individual (a.k.a a matrix from the array scallops$coorddata)? in snippet B?

Code Snippet A
library(geomorph)
data("scallopPLY")
data("scallops")
warpRefMesh(scallopPLY$ply, scallops$coorddata, mshape(scallops$coorddata))

Error in digitspec[1:fixed, ] : incorrect number of dimensions

Code Snippet B
library(geomorph)
data("scallopPLY")
data("scallops")
warpRefMesh(scallopPLY$ply, scallops$coorddata[,,1], mshape(scallops$coorddata))

Finally, I know this is the geomorph mailing list, but I would like to let you know there is a handy little function, read.pts, in the Morpho package (mady by Stefan Schlager) which can read in .pts files directly. This might save you some hassle converting all your files manually first.

Hope this helps!

With kind regards,
Abel

  'file' must be a character string or connection"

This means you are not calling your file name correctly, But without your line of code I do not know what is exactly the mistake.

Emma

messages.body_plain:
Dear Emma,

I’ve used GM sporadically on archaeological data—chipped stone tools.  I’m no more than ordinarily obtuse.  However, in the process of trying to learn geomorph I encounter fundamental problems at the outset.

Please forgive these extremely basic questions but, frankly, your documentation seems, upon my first reading of essential passages, to assume a great deal that it fails to specify in its 139-pp and that new users may not know.  At least this one doesn’t.

I’ve downloaded geomorph, and completed all of pg. 10’s steps.  OK, geomorph works in R.  But let’s move to my own data.  I’m starting from a set of already-digitized 3D LMs and semiLMs for a set of tools, received as a .csv file.  That’s likely a problem, but it’s easy enough to save files under other extensions.  If I read correctly your Sec. 1.6, pp 11-12, it’s a 2D array of 3D data.  But first things first, because I haven’t gotten far enough to find that out.  Instead, I’ve foundered on two more immediate problems:

1.       Exactly what file types does geomorph accept?  Rather than listing a few of the more common ones, pg. 16 refers me to Rohlf 2012.  That’s a commercial document/app that I’m unwilling to spend money on just to find out if .xls or .txt files are acceptable.  Rohlf’s site may provide the Googling the question didn’t help; it rarely does if one doesn’t have three hours or so to wade through oceans of irrelevant sites.  Checking your document again, Sec. 2, top of pg. 15 discusses “At the end” how to import data “as a simple excel-style matrix”.  Reading all of Sec. 2 line-by-line through pg. 21, I never again encountered the word “excel.”  But Sec. 2.4 (pg. 20) seems to be “the end” to which the starting paragraph refers, and it speaks of .txt files.  So, is there instead a simple list of file types that geomorph will accept?

2.       Assuming the problem 1 is solved (pretty basic; let’s hope so), pg. 20 (Sec. 2.4) advises me on how to read in data that aren’t .nts etc.  Useful, sincerely.  But exactly where do I read them in from?  Your “filelist” example tells me that it lists all files “in working directory”.  What is the working directory?  Where is it? How can I copy files held on my dept.’s server to it or read them into it for subsequent reading via filelist?  Can I specify the full path (e.g., “<-read.table (“Q:/…myfile.extension”, header=TRUE, row.names=1…”strings etc.?  If so, OK.  But if that won’t work, there must be some simple way to access files held on C:/ drives or servers in either geomorph or R, then to somehow place them in whatever the “working directory” is so that they can be identified by filename only.  Apologies, but an hour or more of reading sections of your guide didn’t answer that simple question for me.

I also consulted the geomorph wiki which also, frankly, seems unhelpful.  I’m already apprehensive because at the very start I encounter problems with the most fundamental matters.  It’s as though I bought a new car and received the dealer’s advice to use my key/fob to open and start it, without being given the key/fob or told where the car is.

Hoping you can help,

MS

messages.body_plain:
Michael,

Your issues are in a lack of basic understanding of how to input data into R; it is not an issue with geomorph, its help files, or its manual.

First, geomorph does not ‘accept’ any excel format: R does. R also accepts text files, binary files, and other formats.  Second, it is R which requires the user specify in what directory one’s data files may be found (R is not a point-and-click gui package: it is command line, and command line programs require this sort of specification).  As such, it is the user that must learn sufficient R-skills to know how to do this and to bring their data into R.  Once that has been successfully completed, the functions we provide in geomorph allow one to convert the data matrix into an object the analytical functions will be able to recognize.

It is simply unreasonable to think it within the purview of geomorph’s authors to provide basic R skills, along with a package that performs proper morphometric analyses of such data. Likewise, it is incorrect to assume it a ‘failing’ of geomorph when someone cannot bring their data into R.

We happily provide geomorph to the scientific community and do so freely, but one must recognize that we do this as a volunteer service of our time. If one is not satisfied with how the program functions, then one is free to use other available software, or write their own.

Hi Sam,

A few things.

First, those wiki pages are rather outdated: geomorph contains output for quite a few items which previously required post-hoc calculations. These additions make some Wiki pages and their calculations superfluous.

One example is extracting group means. This is obtained in several ways in geomorph, but one is as part of the output in advanced.procD.lm.  For instance running:

Myres<-advanced.procD.lm(f1=shape~groups, f2=~1, groups = groups, data = myGDF)

Myres$LS.means

This will run the model, and the output $LS.means contains the least squares means for the groups. Note that the approach is general and can obtain LS means for models with covariates (see help file).

As to your measurement error issue, as stated in the Wiki, the repeatability equation used was for the simple case of 2 replicates from a single set of images. You have a more complex design, and having more complex input data may require altering these equation to correspond with correct MS terms from the linear model.

To fully appreciate how to implement more general measurement analyses (multiple individuals, multiple photos, multiple measurements, etc.), I first recommend a careful reading of Chapter 9 of Zelditch et al., as well as the paper by Arnqvist and Martensson 1998 (among others).  Here the expected mean squares are discussed, so one can learn how to extract the correct MS components from the factorial anova table and perform the repeatability analysis.

Best,

Hi Sam,

It is quite unsurprising that you will get negative values with your math because you are subtracting larger MS values from smaller ones.  I’m not sure what you are attempting to do.  Maybe Emma will want to chime in about her original example but if I understood it correctly, the point was to examine (as a reduction from 100%) the amount of variation added by having repeated versions of individuals digitized.  The model has two sources: individuals and residuals (replication).  Her example works IF AND ONLY IF the variation among individuals exceeds the variation within individuals.  If measurement error exceeds inter-individual variation, then the repeatability value she suggested could be negative.  To me, this means you have so much measurement error that any other inference might be foolhardy to make.

But none of the models you are showing us here looks like the one she made.  She also mentioned at the end of her discussion that a factorial model can be used when there are multiple photos and multiple digitizations for each photo.  She did not suggest to try to manipulate MS values like you have if this is the case.

It looks to me that you are combining different topics (model types) in attempting to find results.

Mike

> Hi Sam,
>
> It is quite unsurprising that you will get negative values with your math because you are subtracting larger MS values from smaller ones.  I’m not sure what you are attempting to do.  Maybe Emma will want to chime in about her original example but if I understood it correctly, the point was to examine (as a reduction from 100%) the amount of variation added by having repeated versions of individuals digitized.  The model has two sources: individuals and residuals (replication).  Her example works IF AND ONLY IF the variation among individuals exceeds the variation within individuals.  If measurement error exceeds inter-individual variation, then the repeatability value she suggested could be negative.  To me, this means you have so much measurement error that any other inference might be foolhardy to make.
>
> But none of the models you are showing us here looks like the one she made.  She also mentioned at the end of her discussion that a factorial model can be used when there are multiple photos and multiple digitizations for each photo.  She did not suggest to try to manipulate MS values like you have if this is the case.

Sam,

I see a couple of confusing things here.  First, Emma had indicated before (in the tutorial) to use a factorial model.  You model is not a factorial model, as it does not have Ind and Photo as factors; it has only the interaction.  Emma gave the calculation of repeatability - which you are trying to force on this model despite her using it on a different model, ~ Ind - but she did not say that the formula she gave for the simpler model could just be copied and used again on this model.  You are making that assumption and now concluding that you have 5% repeatability (95% measurement error?).  I believe this is not correct.  Finally, with a factorial model, there would be different possible measurements like this, comparing individuals to photos and photos to replicate digitizations on photos.

I realize in the thread you cited, Emma suggested to use just the interaction.  To be honest, I am a bit naïve, as it was Emma’s tutorial.  I just happened to notice that you were trying to use the repeatability calculation that she gave for a model that was ~ Ind for a model that you are using, which is ~Ind:photo and that in her tutorial she never said the calculation stays the same when you change models.  You are still trying to use this.  What I can tell here is that the 5.69% is based on the difference between photos and replicates within photos, so this is not the same as measurement error made on individuals.  I’ll reiterate, the formula you are using appears to apply only to Emma’s simple model of ~Ind and I think with two replicates.  It is not universal, I believe.  (Someone can correct me if I am wrong.)

I am not really qualified to comment further.  I do not understand the repeatability measurement.  If it were me I would simply perform a nested ANOVA and look at the MS and Rsq values for Ind, Photo, Ind:Photo, and Residuals to see if I felt comfortable with my ability to digitize the same way and capture the same “shape” from multiple photos.  Somebody else in our community might have better advice.

Mike

Sam,

Emma’s tutorials were meant as examples, NOT recipes. They were for illustration purposes to provide context for what is found in the primary literature. If someone wishes to alter their data relative to what she demonstrated, then the approach must also be altered in some manner.

However, at that point, it is the responsibility of the user to alter things, not others. In your case, I will reiterate what I stated originally: please go read the primary literature carefully in regards to repeatability analyses, and understand what these approaches are trying to do.  Such analyses require mean-squared values from a factorial model, combined in some manner. That ‘some manner’ depends on the design under investigation. Sometimes it is the same as in the example; sometimes not. Mike and I have tried to be very clear on this.

The point is that one must fully understand and appreciate anova models, what they are, and what they represent, to do this correctly. Otherwise, one ends up with strange results (like negative repeatability measures). There are many examples of repeatability analyses in the literature and quite a few spell out precisely which MS term was used for which component of the analysis.

Maybe Emma will want to chime in about her original example but if I understood it correctly, the point was to examine (as a reduction from 100%) the amount of variation added by having repeated versions of individuals digitized. Sam,
just a quick addition to what Dean and Mike have already commented:

You may also want to consult and follow previous discussions on this googlegroup, as you may find answers that will help you in your particular analysis. The discussion in the link below, motivated relatively recently by a user´s question, came to mind when reading your messages, as it discussed precisely how one may handle repeated designs to evaluate sources of error and variation in the data.

https://groups.google.com/forum/?hl=en#!msg/geomorph-r-package/O-QypQQK59I/CXSIabuiAwAJ;context-place=forum/geomorph-r-package

Again, this is but a piece of the puzzle and you will need to adequately adapt it to your specific data and questions, after you have carefully reviewed basic bibliography on the subject and fully understood how SS and MS work in ANOVA models of this kind. But I think it may provide some useful insights.

Hope this helps,
Antigoni

> However, at that point, it is the responsibility of the user to alter things, not others. In your case, I will reiterate what I stated originally: please go read the primary literature carefully in regards to repeatability analyses, and understand what these approaches are trying to do.  Such analyses require mean-squared values from a factorial model, combined in some manner. That ‘some manner’ depends on the design under investigation. Sometimes it is the same as in the example; sometimes not. Mike and I have tried to be very clear on this.
>
>
>
> The point is that one must fully understand and appreciate anova models, what they are, and what they represent, to do this correctly. Otherwise, one ends up with strange results (like negative repeatability measures). There are many examples of repeatability analyses in the literature and quite a few spell out precisely which MS term was used for which component of the analysis.

I want to perform object symmetry on my data (with semi landmarks) so used gpagen before using bilat.symmetry to specify that I would like object symmetry. All this works fine but I am unable to access my csize on the outputted symmetric data, which I would like to use for the rest of my analysis.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam,

Bilat.symmetry does not output sizes, but you already have them as output from gpagen. For matching symmetry evaluating symmetric and asymmetric shape (and size) makes sense as there are two objects being compared. However, for object symmetry there is a single size per individual, so it is unclear what the symmetric and asymmetric size components would represent in this case. This is why the size anova is not computed in bilat.symmetry for object symmetry.

As for replicates, using 4 per individual is fine; a vector specifying them is provided in the replicate = argument of the function. If you then want to calculate a mean for each individual for other shape analyses, you need to do so on superimposed coordinates.

Hope this helps.

Cheers,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Christy,

As far as I know, this function does not yet exist for the 2-block PLS, but I have run into the same issue.  I have created a work around where I stole some of the source code from the old two.b.pls function and created a monster that I have to hand edit, but that outputs the coordinates at either end of the PLS plot for one axis.  I believe that if Emma wished to do so, she could modify the current function to output the 'pls1.max' and 'pls1.min' at the end of the block to which we could plotreftotarget.  I'm not knowledgeable enough in R to actually bind it as a function myself so I've just been sharing around this code:

###The following block of code was extracted from the two.b.pls function code.  PROVIDING YOU CHANGE THE ***** OBJECT TO THE PLS YOU JUST RAN, It can all be run in a group and the end result will be two objects that we need to warp the ref shape to the max and min values of pls1 for block 1 (the shape coordinate data)

plsnew<-function (x, y, RV = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
{
  x <- as.matrix(x)
  y <- as.matrix(y)
  px <- ncol(x)
  py <- ncol(y)
  pmin <- min(px, py)
  S <- var(cbind(x, y))
  S12 <- matrix(S[1:px, -(1:px)], px, py)
  pls <- La.svd(S12, pmin, pmin)
  U <- pls$u
  V <- t(pls$vt)
  XScores <- x %*% U
  YScores <- y %*% V
  r.pls <- cor(XScores[, 1], YScores[, 1])
  if (RV == TRUE) {
    S11 <- S[1:px, 1:px]
    S22 <- S[-(1:px), -(1:px)]
    RV <- sum(colSums(S12^2))/sqrt(sum(S11^2) * sum(S22^2))
  }
  else RV <- NULL
  if (verbose == TRUE) {
    XScores <- as.matrix(XScores)
    Y <- as.matrix(YScores)
    rownames(U) = colnames(x)
    rownames(V) = colnames(y)
    out <- list(pls.svd = pls, r.pls = r.pls, RV = RV, left.vectors = U,
                right.vectors = V, XScores = XScores, YScores = YScores)
  }
  else out <- r.pls
  out
}

p<-PPLS #********************************CHANGE THIS TO THE NAME OF THE PLS YOU JUST RAN

A1 <- p$A1
A2 <- p$A2
XScores <- p$XScores
YScores <- p$YScores
if (is.matrix(XScores))
  XScores <- XScores[, 1]
if (is.matrix(YScores))
  YScores <- YScores[, 1]
plsRaw <- plsnew(p$A1.matrix, p$A2.matrix, verbose = TRUE)
XScoresRaw <- plsRaw$XScores[, 1]
YScoresRaw <- plsRaw$YScores[, 1]
pc <- prcomp(cbind(XScores, YScores))$x[, 1]
px <- predict(lm(XScores ~ pc))
py <- predict(lm(YScores ~ pc))
pxmax <- max(px)
pxmin <- min(px)
pymax <- max(py)
pymin <- min(py)
pcRaw <- prcomp(cbind(XScoresRaw, YScoresRaw))$x[, 1]
pxRaw <- predict(lm(XScoresRaw ~ pcRaw))
pyRaw <- predict(lm(YScoresRaw ~ pcRaw))
pxmaxRaw <- max(pxRaw)
pxminRaw <- min(pxRaw)
pymaxRaw <- max(pyRaw)
pyminRaw <- min(pyRaw)
if (length(dim(A1)) == 3) {
  A1.ref <- mshape(A1)
  A1.min <- arrayspecs(pxminRaw * p$left.pls.vectors[,
                                                     1], nrow(A1.ref), ncol(A1.ref))[, , 1]
  A1.max <- arrayspecs(pxmaxRaw * p$left.pls.vectors[,
                                                     1], nrow(A1.ref), ncol(A1.ref))[, , 1]
  pls1.min <- A1.ref + A1.min
  pls1.max <- A1.ref + A1.max
  pls1.mid <- A1.ref + 0.5*A1.max
}

#********************************************************************************************END OF BLOCK********************************
#saves the coords we just created as .csv file
write.csv (pls1.max, file = "pls1maxcoords.csv")
write.csv (pls1.min, file = "pls1mincoords.csv")

pls.min <- read.csv("pls1mincoords.csv")

#Now let's visualize the differences between these:
PLS1Max<-plotRefToTarget(M1=ref, M2=pls1.max, mesh = averagemesh, method = c("surface"), links = NULL)
PLS1Min<-plotRefToTarget(M1=ref, M2=pls1.min, mesh = averagemesh, method = c("surface"), links = NULL)

I hope that you can modify this to your needs to output both axes.
Good luck,
~Jasmine

Christy, Jasmine,

Yes, it is true that there is currently no mesh option with plot.pls but there is no need to overwrite code and do something complicated.  The function, shape.predictor, can be used to generate coordinates for plotRefToTarget for any point anywhere in a PLS (or other) plot.  There is an example showing exactly how to do this for PLS on the help page for this function.

To answer your other question, yes, your intuition is correct.  You can save the shapes generated and go straight to plotRefToTarget.  Either way (shape.predictor or export the shapes after the shapes = TRUE argument is used) will give you the coordinates to use in plotRefToTarget.

The reason for this irregularity is that plot.pls has ellipsis capability - meaning that arguments can be passed to other functions - but it is currently set up to pass the arguments to the default plot but not the additional plots for warp grids or meshes.  I’ll try to update this soon, but in the meantime, you can use plotRefToTarget in 1-2 extra steps to make your extreme mesh plots.

Cheers!
Mike

Hello Nadja,

Your plan is nearly perfectly correct except that instead of the $LS.obs.means.dist output from advanced.procD.lm, use $LS.means.  Verify that the means extracted this way have the same row names as the tips on your phylogeny (but the order is not important).  plotGMPhyloMorphoSpace should be able to do the rest.

Good luck and for a “newbie”, your intuition was excellent!

Best,
Mike
